newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Crude Outlook - Little respite for sellers.
newsitem.headline: Asia Crude Outlook - Little respite for sellers.

text.p: Crude trading for the latest months has largely come to an end and market focus is shifting this week to next-month trading, but with little respite seen for the sellers.

Middle East grades, trading for June lifting, are expected to remain weak. The refining capacity on turnaround is to fall in June, but the weakness of Brent is keeping arbitrage opportunities into Asia wide open, so keeping supplies ample.
Traders said China remained the swing factor for the market and whether it would soak up the surplus supplies.
China has purchased in April up to four very large crude carriers (VLCC) of West African Cabinda crude oil and has already purchased a further 900,000 barrels of the crude for May loading.
Traders said the arbitrage would be the key factor depressing demand for key Middle East grades and regional crude.

Brent/Dubai for May was valued late on Friday at $1.65/$1.70 in New York and June at $1.30/$1.45, which traders said would allow West African crude oil and Yemeni crude, which is traded against dated Brent, to flow into Asia.
"I should imagine demand will be stronger in June than it was in May because a lot more refineries are back up," said one senior crude trader. "But West African arbitrage is wide open."
Apart from the huge flow of West African crude oil flowing into Asia, the weakness of Brent is making Yemeni crude attractive.
The first June Masila cargo was traded last week at the official selling price (OSP) plus 15 cents, higher than May cargoes.

Dated Brent in London was valued on Friday at 55 to 45 cents under May futures, not as weak as more than 90-cents discount earlier last week. But the steep contango remains, giving little indication of a firmer market near term, traders said.
Among Middle East grades, Oman could suffer the weakest market in June after traders were disappointed by only a five-cent narrowing in the Dubai/Oman differential to $1.00 for June trading.
"The result of that pittance of a reduction is that June will not be an easy month to trade," one seller said.

Oman for June was being offered in the market at 10 cents under the OSP with bids seen at a small discount. Oman in May, which is expected to be a weaker month than June, traded as low as five cents under the OSP.
Other Middle East differentials came in much more than Oman. Among Asian crude, the light sweet market is facing the most scrutiny with traders expecting prices to weaken further.

The first major sign has come from the Australian Cossack market, where a May cargo traded last week at Tapis quotes less 40 cents, defying an earlier offer from a major on a prompt cargo of quotes flat.
Traders said middle distillates still offered a strong refining margin, owing to gas oil buying of a Singapore trader, which would indicate support for Tapis, a middle distillate yielding crude.
But they said that Tapis has failed to match the global slide in crude prices during the past month, indicating it was overvalued for now.
A producer has most recently traded May Tapis at OSP +23 cents, but Tapis was heard traded for the Banghchak refinery at OSP plus a small premium.
Traders said they expected further pressure on Tapis and Tapis-related crudes to come this week.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65 870 3081)
